arXiv:2610.04920v1 [cs.CV] 04 Oct 2026

PWM: Personalized World Models with
Online Reinforcement Learning

Zhexin Lou   Guancheng Lu   Zeyu Zhang   Yi Zhang   Yang Zhao     Hao Tang Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University   Affiliation: La Trobe University Affiliation: Northwestern University      *Equal contribution. Project lead. Corresponding author: bjdxtanghao@gmail.com
Abstract

Pretrained world models can generate diverse environments, yet users often want to explore a particular scene specified by their own video. This requires learning the scene’s visual identity while retaining the quality of action-conditioned generation. We introduce Personalized World Models (PWM), a framework for customizing interactive world models from short scene videos through online reinforcement learning. In PWM, the support trajectory and its associated controls provide reward feedback on continuations sampled from the current policy. In the GRPO instantiation, group-relative optimization updates a compact LoRA adapter using a unified reward for scene appearance, visual continuity, and motion, while base-policy anchoring regularizes changes to the pretrained generation prior of a frozen Yume-5B backbone. The same adaptation procedure is applied across real and rendered environments. We also instantiate PWM with DiffusionNFT as an alternative reward-guided optimization method for learning the scene-specific adapter. We also introduce PWM-Bench, comprising 150 customization tasks across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming, with paired evaluation on held-out continuations. The GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve customization over native Yume in 71.3% and 65.3% of the evaluated scenes, respectively, with positive mean gains across all three domains. For the GRPO instantiation, matched SFT comparisons further demonstrate higher mean customization gains and better mean image-quality scores in every domain, while retaining frame-level visual quality close to the pretrained model. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/PWM. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/PWM.

1 Introduction

Interactive world models enable users to explore environments through action-conditioned video generation. Recent systems combine pretrained visual generation priors with user controls and autoregressive rollout, supporting interactive exploration across diverse environments (Yu et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2026). Personalizing this experience introduces a concrete requirement: the generated world should retain the identity of the environment provided by the user. For a particular interior, outdoor location, or game scene, its characteristic appearance and content should remain recognizable as the generated trajectory progresses.

Personalization methods have demonstrated that pretrained generators can acquire visual identity from limited reference observations (Ruiz et al., 2023). Interactive world generation extends this objective to action-conditioned continuations. A short support video provides observations of a scene’s materials, lighting, visual style, and characteristic content. Successful customization should therefore strengthen fidelity to the target environment while retaining the visual quality of the underlying generator.

Reward-based optimization provides a way to express preferences directly on generated images and videos (Xue et al., 2025). For scene customization, the support trajectory can supply the reference needed to evaluate those outputs: whether they match the environment’s appearance and whether their visual evolution is consistent with the observed trajectory.

We introduce Personalized World Models (PWM), a framework for per-scene customization through online reinforcement learning. Given a short support trajectory and its controls, PWM learns a compact LoRA adapter on a frozen Yume-5B backbone. The current policy samples groups of candidate continuations, and reward feedback derived from the support trajectory guides updates to the scene-specific adapter. We instantiate this framework with GRPO and DiffusionNFT as alternative reward-guided optimization methods. Online learning here refers to collecting fresh rollouts from the current policy during adaptation.

Both instantiations use native generation windows, the same adapter capacity, and a shared reward for scene appearance, visual continuity, and motion. The GRPO instantiation additionally uses a base-policy anchor. Optimization and checkpoint-averaging settings are fixed across scenes within each instantiation.

To evaluate this capability, we introduce PWM-Bench, a suite of 150 per-scene customization tasks spanning Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. Each task provides an 80-frame support segment and a temporally later, non-overlapping 145-frame test continuation. The benchmark evaluates scene fidelity through appearance agreement and an entity-based hallucination penalty, complemented by frame-level image-quality measurements. Comparisons use three paired random seeds per scene under shared initial context, controls, and generation settings.

Across PWM-Bench, the GRPO instantiation of PWM improves customization over native Yume in 107 of 150 scenes, with a mean relative gain of 6.39%. The DiffusionNFT instantiation improves 98 of 150 scenes, with a mean relative gain of 5.22%. Both instantiations achieve positive mean gains in every domain. Compared with matched SFT, the GRPO instantiation increases the fraction of scenes improved over Native from 57.3% to 71.3% and achieves higher mean customization gains across all three domains. It also obtains better domain-level means than SFT on MUSIQ, NIQE, and BRISQUE, while remaining close to native Yume in these frame-level quality measures.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce PWM, a per-scene customization framework that learns a compact adapter from a short support trajectory through online reinforcement learning on a frozen interactive world model, instantiated with GRPO and DiffusionNFT.

  • •

    We introduce PWM-Bench, comprising 150 customization tasks across three first-person domains, with held-out continuations and a shared protocol for evaluating scene fidelity and visual quality.

  • •

    We demonstrate positive average customization gains over native Yume across all three domains with both optimization methods. Matched SFT comparisons show that the GRPO instantiation benefits more scenes and achieves better mean image-quality scores.

2 Related Work

Interactive world models.

Interactive world generation combines visual synthesis with action control to produce trajectories that respond to user inputs. GameFactory (Yu et al., 2025) learns action control from game videos and uses a domain adapter with multi-phase training to transfer this capability to open-domain scenes. Yume (Mao et al., 2025) combines camera control with autoregressive video generation, while Yume-1.5 (Mao et al., 2026) develops context compression and text-controlled interaction for continuous world exploration. These advances establish a foundation for generating and navigating diverse environments. PWM studies how to specialize such a pretrained model to a particular observed scene. Given a short support trajectory, it learns a compact scene adapter for subsequent action-conditioned generation in the same environment.

Personalization of generative models.

Personalization adapts a generative prior to visual content specified by limited reference observations. DreamBooth (Ruiz et al., 2023) learns a subject from a few images and synthesizes that subject in new contexts. Tune-A-Video (Wu et al., 2023) extends adaptation from limited observations to video generation by tuning an image diffusion model on a single text–video pair. Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) support this adaptation through trainable low-rank updates to frozen pretrained weights. PWM applies scene-level personalization to an interactive world model: the support video provides observations of the target environment, and the learned adapter is evaluated on a temporally held-out continuation under action controls.

Reinforcement learning for visual generation.

Reward-based fine-tuning adapts visual generators to objectives defined on their outputs. DDPO (Black et al., 2024) treats iterative denoising as a sequential decision process and applies policy gradients to optimize sample-level rewards. VADER (Prabhudesai et al., 2024) optimizes video generation by propagating gradients from differentiable reward models. DanceGRPO (Xue et al., 2025) applies group-relative policy optimization to diffusion and rectified-flow models across image and video generation. DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026) performs online reward-guided optimization through the forward noising process, incorporating positive and negative learning signals into a flow-matching objective without requiring likelihood estimation. Building on this line of work, PWM obtains reward feedback from the target scene’s support trajectory and updates a scene-specific adapter using online rollouts. We instantiate PWM with GRPO and DiffusionNFT, using the same scene-level task, adapter capacity, and reward definition. The reward combines visual agreement with initial-frame consistency and motion magnitude matching, connecting reward-based optimization to the scene customization objective.

Weight averaging.

Weight averaging combines parameter states into a single model. Stochastic Weight Averaging (Izmailov et al., 2018) averages weights along a training trajectory, while Model Soups (Wortsman et al., 2022) averages models fine-tuned from a shared pretrained initialization. PWM uses this idea within each scene’s adaptation run, averaging adapter checkpoints to retain a single compact adapter for inference. Each optimization instantiation uses a checkpoint-averaging rule that is fixed across scenes and does not use held-out test frames.

3 Method

We propose PWM, a per-scene personalization approach for interactive world models. Given a short preceding trajectory, PWM trains a scene-specific LoRA on frozen Yume-5B to transfer scene knowledge to a subsequent trajectory. The core objectives are visual identity tailored to the target scene, persistent spatial layout, and action responsiveness, while retaining the general action and control priors of the pretrained world model. For this reason, PWM combines scene-specific low-rank parameterization, online reward-guided optimization with GRPO or DiffusionNFT based on native generation windows, a unified reward that balances scene fidelity and motion, and a weight averaging strategy that does not require selecting a single checkpoint.

Figure 2 summarizes the shared adaptation pipeline and the two online optimization instantiations.

3.1 Preliminaries: Yume, GRPO, and DiffusionNFT

Yume interactive world model.

Yume-1.5 (Mao et al., 2026) extends a pretrained video generator into an action-command-controllable interactive world model. Given a compressed visual history hth_{t} and a sequence utu_{t} containing action commands for generation window tt, the frozen Yume-5B model, parameterized by θ0\theta_{0}, generates the next video segment according to

Xt∼pθ0​(Xt∣ht,ut).X_{t}\sim p_{\theta_{0}}(X_{t}\mid h_{t},u_{t}). (1)

The control sequence combines discrete translation and camera commands with continuous motion magnitudes. Each generated segment is incorporated into the visual history to condition the subsequent window, resulting in a segment-level autoregressive interaction trajectory. PWM keeps θ0\theta_{0} frozen and learns only a scene-specific low-rank adapter.

Group Relative Policy Optimization.

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) estimates advantages by comparing a group of samples generated under the same condition, thereby eliminating the need for a learned critic (Shao et al., 2024). Given a condition cc, GRPO samples GG trajectories from an old-policy snapshot and normalizes their outcome rewards within the group:

τi∼πθold(⋅∣c),A^i=ri−r¯sr,i=1,…,G,\tau_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(\cdot\mid c),\qquad\widehat{A}_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\overline{r}}{s_{r}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,G, (2)

where r¯\overline{r} and srs_{r} denote the mean and standard deviation of {rj}j=1G\{r_{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}. Under outcome-level supervision, the same A^i\widehat{A}_{i} is assigned to every decision step along trajectory τi\tau_{i}.

Let KiK_{i} be the number of decision steps in τi\tau_{i}. GRPO optimizes the empirical clipped surrogate

J^clip​(θ)=1G∑i=1G1Ki∑k=1Kimin(ρi,k(θ)A^i,OPENclip⁡(ρi,k​(θ),1−εclip,1+εclip)​A^i),ρi,k​(θ)=πθ​(ai,k∣si,k)πθold​(ai,k∣si,k).\begin{split}\widehat{J}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta)&=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\min\Bigl(\rho_{i,k}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{i},\,\\ &\qquad\qquad\operatorname{clip}\bigl(\rho_{i,k}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\bigr)\widehat{A}_{i}\Bigr),\\ \rho_{i,k}(\theta)&=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{i,k}\mid s_{i,k})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,k}\mid s_{i,k})}.\end{split} (3)

GRPO therefore replaces a learned critic with a group-reward baseline rather than removing the baseline altogether. Its original formulation additionally regularizes the policy toward a separate reference policy πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The GRPO instantiation of PWM instead employs the base-policy anchor introduced in Section 3.2.

Policy interpretation of diffusion and flow sampling.

Following DDPO and DanceGRPO (Black et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2025), iterative diffusion and rectified-flow sampling can be formulated as a finite-horizon Markov decision process. Let ct=(ht,ut)c_{t}=(h_{t},u_{t}) denote the visual history and control condition for video window tt. After stochasticizing the reverse-time transition, the state, action, and policy at denoising step kk are defined as

st,k=(ct,k,zt,k),at,k=zt,k−1,πθ​(at,k∣st,k)=pθ​(zt,k−1∣zt,k,ct).\begin{gathered}s_{t,k}=(c_{t},k,z_{t,k}),\qquad a_{t,k}=z_{t,k-1},\\ \pi_{\theta}(a_{t,k}\mid s_{t,k})=p_{\theta}(z_{t,k-1}\mid z_{t,k},c_{t}).\end{gathered} (4)

A complete latent trajectory τt=(zt,K,…,zt,0)\tau_{t}=(z_{t,K},\ldots,z_{t,0}) produces one video segment and receives a terminal reward. Under group-relative optimization, the resulting trajectory advantage is assigned to each denoising transition. Here, kk indexes the internal denoising process, whereas tt indexes the external sequence of autoregressive video windows.

We use online to mean that each data-collection round collects fresh trajectories from the latest behavior-policy snapshot. It does not refer to continual adaptation after deployment.

DiffusionNFT.

DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026) performs online reward-guided optimization through a forward-process flow-matching objective. Generated samples are assigned reward-dependent weights, which determine their contributions to positive and negative learning branches. These branches are constructed from the current model’s velocity prediction and a fixed behavior-policy prediction, allowing reward-guided updates without estimating sampling-trajectory likelihoods. PWM instantiates this objective for scene-specific LoRA adaptation, as described in Section 3.3.

Problem Formulation: Per-scene Customization

Let a scene ss be a temporally ordered controlled trajectory 𝒟s={(xt,ut)}t=1T\mathcal{D}_{s}=\{(x_{t},u_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T}, where xtx_{t} is a video frame and utu_{t} contains translation, camera, and continuous motion controls. A support prefix 𝒟ssup\mathcal{D}_{s}^{\mathrm{sup}} is available for adaptation. The goal is to specialize the model to the persistent identity of ss and transfer that knowledge to a later, unseen portion of the same scene. No frame from the future evaluation portion is used for optimization or checkpoint construction.

We start from a frozen Yume-5B world model with parameters θ0\theta_{0}. For each scene, PWM learns an independent rank-88 LoRA adapter Δ​θs\Delta\theta_{s} (20.2M trainable parameters), while all backbone parameters remain fixed. The resulting policy is πθ0+Δ​θs\pi_{\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{s}}. This factorization assigns complementary roles to the two parameter sets: the frozen backbone supplies the general action-conditioned generation prior, whereas the adapter stores knowledge specific to the target scene. The current paper uses the same adapter capacity for both optimization methods, every scene, and every first-person domain.

3.2 Per-scene Customization via Online GRPO

Learning in the deployment geometry.

PWM trains directly with Yume’s native 2929-frame generation window. We cover the support trajectory with six overlapping windows whose start indices are [0,9,18,27,36,45][0,9,18,27,36,45]. Each window is initialized by its real first frame and is conditioned on the controls measured for that window. Training and deployment therefore share the same temporal geometry; no auxiliary short-window policy is introduced.

On-policy group-relative optimization.

PWM instantiates the GRPO update in Eq. 3 with a group of G=4G=4 diffusion trajectories for each support window. The trajectories share the initial latent noise to control nuisance variation while retaining independent stochastic SDE transitions. Because the unified reward contains components with different numerical scales, we normalize each component separately before combining their advantages. For reward component mm and rollout ii, we compute

Ai=∑mαm​Ri,m−μmσm+ε,(μm,σm)=MeanStdj=1G⁡[Rj,m],A_{i}=\sum_{m}\alpha_{m}\frac{R_{i,m}-\mu_{m}}{\sigma_{m}+\varepsilon},\qquad(\mu_{m},\sigma_{m})=\operatorname{MeanStd}_{j=1}^{G}\!\left[R_{j,m}\right], (5)

where αm\alpha_{m} is the weight of component mm in Eq. (12). The resulting AiA_{i} replaces the scalar-reward advantage A^i\widehat{A}_{i} in Eq. (3). This component-wise normalization prevents a reward term from dominating the policy update merely because of its numerical scale.

We use ε=10−6\varepsilon=10^{-6} and set a component’s contribution to zero when its within-group standard deviation is below 10−310^{-3} (Appendix A.3).

In the PWM implementation, the clipped surrogate uses ρ~i,k=ρi,k1/d\widetilde{\rho}_{i,k}=\rho_{i,k}^{1/d}, computed from Gaussian log densities averaged over the dd scalar latent elements in the generated region (Appendix A.3).

Noise-robust score-on-mean.

In few-step diffusion sampling, the final stochastic transition can inject visible noise into the decoded rollout. Scoring that sample directly can make the relative advantage reflect the last noise draw rather than scene content. PWM therefore separates the trajectory used for policy learning from the video used for reward measurement. For the final transition

zi′=μθ​(zi,cs)+σ​ϵi,z_{i}^{\prime}=\mu_{\theta}(z_{i},c_{s})+\sigma\epsilon_{i}, (6)

the policy likelihood is evaluated at the sampled state zi′z_{i}^{\prime}, but the reward is evaluated on the decoded conditional mean x~i=Dec⁡(μθ​(zi,cs))\widetilde{x}_{i}=\operatorname{Dec}(\mu_{\theta}(z_{i},c_{s})). Thus, exploration remains stochastic and on-policy, while rollout ranking is based on a noise-reduced estimate of scene content.

Finally, the GRPO instantiation of PWM anchors every updated transition to the frozen base model. Let μθ​(si,k)\mu_{\theta}(s_{i,k}) and μθ0​(si,k)\mu_{\theta_{0}}(s_{i,k}) denote the transition means predicted with the adapter enabled and disabled, respectively, at the same denoising state. The GRPO objective used in PWM is

ℒPWM\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PWM}} =−J^clip​(θ0+Δ​θs)\displaystyle=-\widehat{J}_{\mathrm{clip}}(\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{s}) (7)
+λG∑i=1G1Ki∑k=1Ki1d‖μθ0+Δ​θs(si,k)−μθ0(si,k)‖22.\displaystyle+\frac{\lambda}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{K_{i}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{i}}\frac{1}{d}\left\|\mu_{\theta_{0}+\Delta\theta_{s}}(s_{i,k})-\mu_{\theta_{0}}(s_{i,k})\right\|_{2}^{2}.

This mean-matching anchor preserves the pretrained transition dynamics while the group-relative advantage moves the adapter toward better continuations for the target scene. We use four Euler denoising steps, four PPO passes per rollout group, λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, a learning rate of 10−410^{-4}, and SDE temperature β=0.5\beta=0.5. For the GRPO instantiation, every scene is trained for eight epochs with the same configuration.

3.3 Per-scene Customization via DiffusionNFT

We also instantiate PWM with DiffusionNFT (Zheng et al., 2026), which incorporates reward feedback through a forward-process flow-matching objective. This instantiation uses the same frozen Yume-5B backbone, LoRA capacity, six native support windows, and unified reward as the GRPO instantiation.

Online sampling and reward normalization.

For each support window, we sample G=4G=4 continuations with independent initial latent noise and compute their rewards using the same score-on-mean procedure. Let RiR_{i} be the scalar reward from Eq. (12), and let R¯\overline{R} be its mean within the current window’s rollout group. We convert each reward into a bounded weight

qi=12+12​clip⁡(Ri−R¯Zs,−1,1),q_{i}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{clip}\left(\frac{R_{i}-\overline{R}}{Z_{s}},-1,1\right), (8)

where ZsZ_{s} is the running standard deviation of rollout rewards collected during adaptation of scene ss, with a lower bound of 10−310^{-3}.

Reward-guided flow matching.

Let zi0z_{i}^{0} denote the generated latent segment used for reward measurement. We sample a noise level σ\sigma from the four levels of the generation schedule and draw fresh Gaussian noise:

ziσ=(1−σ)zi0+σϵ,ϵ∼𝒩(0,I),vi⋆=ϵ−zi0.\begin{gathered}z_{i}^{\sigma}=(1-\sigma)z_{i}^{0}+\sigma\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\\ v_{i}^{\star}=\epsilon-z_{i}^{0}.\end{gathered} (9)

The visual history and action condition are kept fixed. Let vθv_{\theta} be the current velocity prediction at (ziσ,σ,ct)(z_{i}^{\sigma},\sigma,c_{t}) and voldv_{\mathrm{old}} the prediction cached before the update. DiffusionNFT defines

vi+\displaystyle v_{i}^{+} =(1−βNFT)​vold+βNFT​vθ,\displaystyle=(1-\beta_{\mathrm{NFT}})v_{\mathrm{old}}+\beta_{\mathrm{NFT}}v_{\theta}, (10)
vi−\displaystyle v_{i}^{-} =(1+βNFT)​vold−βNFT​vθ,\displaystyle=(1+\beta_{\mathrm{NFT}})v_{\mathrm{old}}-\beta_{\mathrm{NFT}}v_{\theta},

and minimizes

ℒNFT=𝔼i,σ,ϵ[\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{i,\sigma,\epsilon}\Big[ qi​MSE⁡(vi+,vi⋆)\displaystyle q_{i}\,\operatorname{MSE}(v_{i}^{+},v_{i}^{\star}) (11)
+(1−qi)MSE(vi−,vi⋆)].\displaystyle+(1-q_{i})\,\operatorname{MSE}(v_{i}^{-},v_{i}^{\star})\Big].

Here, MSE\operatorname{MSE} averages over latent elements, and gradients are taken only through vθv_{\theta}. The reward weights determine the contribution of the positive and negative branches to the adapter update.

We collect 2424 rollouts across the six support windows and draw two noise-level/noise pairs per rollout. We perform four optimization passes over this collected batch, accumulating gradients across windows. The cached behavior predictions remain fixed during these passes. We use βNFT=0.5\beta_{\mathrm{NFT}}=0.5, a learning rate of 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}, and eight training epochs. This instantiation uses the current behavior-policy snapshot without an EMA teacher or an additional base-policy anchor.

3.4 A Unified Reward Across Domains

Both the GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM use one reward for all scenes and first-person domains:

R=0.50​Rgt+0.30​Rlpips+0.10​Rcross+0.10​Rdyn.R=0.50\,R_{\mathrm{gt}}+0.30\,R_{\mathrm{lpips}}+0.10\,R_{\mathrm{cross}}+0.10\,R_{\mathrm{dyn}}. (12)

The four terms give the optimizer distinct responsibilities. RgtR_{\mathrm{gt}} measures spatially aligned DINO feature agreement between the generated segment and the real continuation of the support window. RlpipsR_{\mathrm{lpips}} is one minus their LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018) distance and therefore preserves perceptual appearance. Both terms are computed per frame and aggregated as 0.70.7 times the temporal mean plus 0.30.3 times the minimum, so a short failure cannot be hidden by otherwise strong frames. RcrossR_{\mathrm{cross}} measures DINO feature agreement between the first generated frame and the window’s ground-truth first frame. Finally, RdynR_{\mathrm{dyn}} rewards agreement between generated and real optical-flow magnitudes, so appearance fidelity cannot be obtained by suppressing motion. Together, the first two terms specify what the scene should look like, while the latter two constrain how a valid continuation should evolve.

All reward references are drawn exclusively from the support trajectory. We do not tune reward weights per scene or per domain, and the evaluation metric is separate from this training reward (Section 4). This separation makes PWM a single customization procedure rather than a collection of scene-specific reward recipes.

GRPO combines component-wise normalized advantages through Eq. (5), while DiffusionNFT uses the combined scalar reward through Eq. (8).

3.5 Checkpoint Soup

Small-data policy optimization can visit useful but different adapter states across epochs. Selecting one of them per scene would introduce an additional selection rule and could couple the delivered model to a noisy validation estimate. For both GRPO and DiffusionNFT, PWM instead saves the adapter at every epoch and averages all eight checkpoints element-wise:

Δ​θ¯s=18​∑e=18Δ​θs(e).\overline{\Delta\theta}_{s}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{e=1}^{8}\Delta\theta_{s}^{(e)}. (13)

Here, averaging is applied to the corresponding stored LoRA factor tensors. This checkpoint soup (Wortsman et al., 2022) is the final scene model. Because factor-wise averaging preserves the adapter’s rank and architecture, PWM still deploys one compact adapter and incurs no additional inference cost. The delivery rule is fixed across scenes and does not inspect the future test trajectory.

4 PWM-Bench

Customization promises that the model reproduces the persistent identity of this scene — its layout, materials, and sense of place — on a continuation it has never observed. Our benchmark evaluates this promise directly: each generated rollout is scored against the held-out ground-truth continuation of its own scene.

Figure 3 shows representative training-support frames from the three domains of PWM-Bench.

4.1 Customization-Fidelity Score

For a generated rollout g1:Tg_{1:T} and the ground-truth test segment x1:Tx_{1:T} (T=145T{=}145 frames), the score is

S\displaystyle S =Dpair+0.5​Dhall,\displaystyle=D_{\mathrm{pair}}+0.5\,D_{\mathrm{hall}}, (14)
Dpair\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{pair}} =1T​∑t=1T(1−cos⁡(ϕ⁡(gt),ϕ⁡(xt))),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Bigl(1-\cos\bigl(\phi(g_{t}),\phi(x_{t})\bigr)\Bigr), (15)
Dhall\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{hall}} =1T​∑t=1T𝟏​[gt​ contains an entity class absent from ​x1],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbf{1}\bigl[g_{t}\text{ contains an entity class absent from }x_{1}\bigr], (16)

where ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) is the DINOv2 class-token embedding (Oquab et al., 2024). Lower SS indicates higher fidelity to the scene’s true continuation.

DpairD_{\mathrm{pair}} measures appearance fidelity as the average feature distance between generated and ground-truth frames at the same timestep, in the DINO feature space commonly used to measure fidelity in personalized generation (Ruiz et al., 2023). We use a time-aligned comparison over the full horizon, rather than a distributional one, because distributional metrics can reward plausible but generic continuations; matching the specific scene as it unfolds is precisely what customization is expected to deliver.

DhallD_{\mathrm{hall}} measures the fraction of generated frames containing an entity class (person, vehicle, or animal, detected by zero-shot CLIP (Radford et al., 2021)) that is absent from the first frame of the ground-truth test segment. It serves as a proxy for unexpected entity introduction relative to the initial scene. The detection rules and thresholds are specified in Appendix C.4.

Both PWM instantiations and Yume are scored by the same pipeline, with identical captions, initial context, and generation horizon. For each instantiation mm, we report the paired difference

Δm=S⁡(m)−S⁡(Yume),\Delta_{m}=S(m)-S(\mathrm{Yume}), (17)

where mm denotes PWM (GRPO) or PWM (DiffusionNFT). A negative Δm\Delta_{m} indicates improved customization over Yume.

4.2 Scoring Protocol

Each scene is evaluated with three random seeds, shared across Yume and both PWM instantiations, under deterministic inference. For each instantiation, a scene counts as improved if its mean paired difference against Yume over the three seeds is negative. We report improvement rates and mean and maximum scene-level relative gains by domain.

Adaptation uses only the support windows, and evaluation uses only the held-out test segment, so no evaluated frame is seen during training. Both PWM instantiations are evaluated on the same fixed set of scenes.

5 Experimental Setup

5.1 Cross-domain Evaluation Suite

We evaluate 150 independent customization tasks across three first-person domains: 50 outdoor walking scenes, 50 indoor walking scenes, and 50 Minecraft scenes (Table 1). Each task has its own support trajectory, scene adapter, and held-out test trajectory.

Real-world videos come from the visual–inertial odometry (VIO) annotated subset of EgoVid-5M (Wang et al., 2025), YouTube, and, for Indoor, InCrowd-VI (Bamdad et al., 2024). YouTube camera motion is estimated from video and mapped to the shared control representation.

Following GameFactory’s (Yu et al., 2025) automated collection paradigm, our scripted agents record Minecraft videos and synchronized locomotion and camera controls in MineDojo (Fan et al., 2022).

5.2 Per-scene Task Construction

Each task contains an 80-frame support segment and a temporally later, non-overlapping 145-frame test segment from the same scene. PWM adapts independently on each support segment and evaluates the resulting adapter on its held-out continuation.

We use a shared control interface across all three domains. Each video window is conditioned on translation commands (W/A/S/D), a camera-direction token, and three continuous motion magnitudes. For EgoVid-5M, these annotations are obtained from the associated VIO trajectory. For YouTube videos, they are derived from estimated camera motion. For Minecraft, they are recorded directly from the scripted agents.

The same source-side quality criteria are applied across domains. The retained tasks provide continuous and non-degenerate camera motion, consistent scene identity across the support and test segments, and agreement between the control annotations and observed visual motion.

5.3 Controlled Comparisons

We compare PWM with native Yume-5B using the same 29-frame autoregressive generation process, initial visual context, controls, decoding configuration, and rollout horizon. Native Yume uses the same inference pipeline with the scene adapter disabled, isolating the effect of per-scene adaptation.

We additionally compare PWM with a matched SFT-LoRA baseline in the reinforcement-learning ablation. SFT-LoRA uses the same frozen Yume-5B backbone, LoRA capacity, support data, control annotations, optimization budget, and evaluation protocol as PWM. This comparison isolates the contribution of online GRPO beyond scene-specific parameter updates alone.

5.4 Shared Training and Evaluation Configuration

All videos are processed at a resolution of 832×480832\times 480. Each scene is adapted independently with a rank-8 LoRA using α=16\alpha=16, corresponding to 20.2M trainable parameters. We instantiate PWM with GRPO and DiffusionNFT, as described in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. Both instantiations use the same adapter capacity and unified reward in Eq. (12), with checkpoint averaging described in Section 3.5. Within each instantiation, the optimization configuration and checkpoint-averaging rule are fixed across all 150 tasks.

Evaluation follows Section 4.2. Each scene is evaluated with three paired random seeds, {42,123,777}\{42,123,777\}, shared between PWM and native Yume under deterministic inference. Both methods generate the full 145-frame test trajectory. Seed-level paired differences are first averaged within each scene, and every scene contributes once to its domain and to the overall benchmark.

6 Experiments

We evaluate PWM along three dimensions: customization gains over native Yume, the contribution of reinforcement learning beyond supervised adaptation, and visual quality after customization. The evaluation covers 150 scenes across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming, with three paired generation seeds per scene. All customization scores are computed over the complete 145-frame held-out continuation, following Section 5.

6.1 Scene Customization across Domains

Scene appearance and content retention.

Figure 4 illustrates scene customization in a shopping-mall continuation. Both PWM instantiations retain shop displays, while Yume replaces them with window-like structures in later frames.

Measuring customization benefit.

We quantify customization benefit as the relative reduction in the score SS defined in Eq. (14). For scene ss and method mm, let S¯sm\bar{S}_{s}^{m} denote the score averaged over the three generation seeds. The scene-level gain, expressed as a percentage, is

gs​(m)=100​S¯sNative−S¯smS¯sNative.g_{s}(m)=100\,\frac{\bar{S}_{s}^{\mathrm{Native}}-\bar{S}_{s}^{m}}{\bar{S}_{s}^{\mathrm{Native}}}. (18)

Positive values indicate improved customization over Native. We report the mean gain across all evaluated scenes, the maximum scene-level gain, and the fraction of scenes with gs​(m)>0g_{s}(m)>0. Every scene receives equal weight, and negative gains are included in the average. Both the mean and maximum are computed after averaging the three seeds within each scene.

Positive gains across real and rendered environments.

The GRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve customization in 107 and 98 of the 150 evaluated scenes, respectively, achieving mean relative gains of 6.39%6.39\% and 5.22%5.22\% over native Yume (Table 2). The corresponding improvement rates are 71.3%71.3\% and 65.3%65.3\%. Both instantiations achieve positive mean gains across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. These results support the effectiveness of per-scene customization across real and rendered environments using either online reward-guided optimization method.

Benefits beyond the strongest examples.

For the GRPO instantiation, the largest scene-level gains reach 49.00%49.00\% in Indoor, 75.11%75.11\% in Outdoor, and 28.66%28.66\% in Gaming. The median gains are also positive in all three domains: 5.18%5.18\%, 5.82%5.82\%, and 8.18%8.18\%, respectively. Together, the average gain, median gain, and improvement frequency show that the observed customization benefit extends beyond a few highly successful examples.

Snow-cover retention in Gaming.

Figure 6 complements the indoor example with a rendered environment: both PWM instantiations retain snow-covered ground in the selected continuations.

Object hallucination.

Figure 5 shows a local object hallucination: a human face appears on the blue equipment in Yume, while both PWM instantiations retain its equipment appearance.

6.2 The Benefit of Reinforcement Learning

Comparison with matched supervised adaptation.

We assess online RL against matched SFT-LoRA under the settings in Section 5.3. Customization gains and improved-scene counts are measured against the same native Yume baseline.

Figure 7 provides a qualitative comparison of Native Yume, SFT, and both PWM instantiations. In this outdoor example, both PWM instantiations retain visible passage space as generation progresses.

Higher average customization benefit.

Both the DanceGRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM achieve higher mean gains than SFT in every domain (Table 3). In Indoor and Outdoor, both instantiations achieve positive mean gains, compared with negative mean gains for SFT. In Gaming, the mean gain increases from 6.08%6.08\% with SFT to 7.91%7.91\% with DanceGRPO and 6.35%6.35\% with DiffusionNFT. Across all 150 scenes, the mean gain rises from −8.39%-8.39\% with SFT to +6.39%+6.39\% with DanceGRPO and +5.22%+5.22\% with DiffusionNFT.

Scene-level improvement coverage.

Across all 150 scenes, the DanceGRPO and DiffusionNFT instantiations of PWM improve over Native in 107 and 98 scenes, respectively, compared with 86 scenes for SFT. The corresponding improvement rates are 71.3%71.3\%, 65.3%65.3\%, and 57.3%57.3\%. Together with the higher mean gains across all three domains, these results show that both PWM instantiations deliver stronger average customization and benefit a larger fraction of the overall evaluation suite than SFT.

The matched SFT comparison examines how support observations are converted into a scene-specific generation policy. SFT optimizes a supervised diffusion objective on the observed support windows. PWM instead samples continuations from the current policy and uses their relative rewards to guide adaptation. The learning signal therefore depends on what the adapted model actually generates under the support conditions.

6.3 Preserving Visual Quality

Figure 8 illustrates this contrast: SFT exhibits visible blur and repetitive texture artifacts, while PWM (DanceGRPO) retains natural-looking scene appearance in the selected examples.

Quality assessment alongside customization.

We complement the customization score with three no-reference image-quality metrics: MUSIQ-SPAQ (Ke et al., 2021), NIQE (Mittal et al., 2013), and BRISQUE (Mittal et al., 2012). These metrics characterize frame-level visual quality, while SS evaluates scene-specific customization. MUSIQ uses all frames; NIQE and BRISQUE use 19 uniformly sampled frames, including the first and last. Scores are averaged over frames, seeds, and scenes, in that order. Native Yume provides a reference for the pretrained model’s visual quality.

Quality close to Native after customization.

PWM outperforms SFT on the domain means of all three reported image-quality metrics (Table 4). In Indoor, MUSIQ increases from 47.2647.26 with SFT to 59.0659.06 with PWM, compared with 58.9358.93 for Native. In Outdoor, BRISQUE improves from 33.5833.58 to 23.2423.24, close to Native’s 22.6622.66. In Gaming, NIQE improves from 5.905.90 to 3.823.82, compared with 3.813.81 for Native. Across individual scenes, MUSIQ favors PWM over SFT in 123 of 150 cases, and NIQE does so in 132 cases.

Scene identity and image quality provide complementary evidence. The customization score evaluates agreement with the target scene, while the image-quality metrics characterize frame-level appearance. Together, Tables 2 and 4 support the intended benefit of PWM: stronger fidelity to the target scene with frame-level quality close to native Yume.

7 Conclusion and Future Work

We introduced PWM, a framework for customizing a pretrained interactive world model to an individual scene through online reinforcement learning. PWM turns a short support trajectory into a compact LoRA adapter using native-window generation, a shared reward, and a fixed checkpoint-averaging rule. We also introduced PWM-Bench to evaluate per-scene customization across Indoor, Outdoor, and Gaming. Across the evaluated suite, PWM improves customization over native Yume in 107 of 150 scenes. The matched SFT comparison further demonstrates higher mean customization gains and broader scene-level benefits, alongside visual quality close to the pretrained model.

Future work will extend this approach to longer interaction horizons and richer support trajectories, enabling scene customization over more extensive exploration.

Reproducibility Statement

Section 5 specifies task construction and the shared experimental protocol. Appendices A–C provide optimization settings, reward definitions, and scoring details. Evaluation uses three paired seeds on held-out continuations, with no test frames used for adaptation or checkpoint construction.

Appendix A Implementation Details

This appendix describes the DanceGRPO implementation. DiffusionNFT follows Section 3.3. The checkpoint averaging procedure described below applies to both instantiations. The four reward components are specified in Appendix B.

A.1 Adaptation Configuration

For each scene, we train one LoRA adapter on the frozen Yume-5B backbone. The adapter is shared across six overlapping support windows of 2929 frames, starting at zero-based indices [0,9,18,27,36,45][0,9,18,27,36,45]. Each window is conditioned on its own ground-truth first frame and corresponding control caption. Windows are processed in this order, with adapter updates carried forward within the scene.

For each window, the current policy generates a group of G=4G=4 trajectories using K=4K=4 stochastic denoising steps. We compute the trajectory advantages and perform four optimization passes on the collected group. Each pass accumulates gradients over all G​KGK transitions before taking one optimizer step. We train for eight epochs and save the adapter after each complete pass through the six windows. This gives 4848 rollout groups and 192192 optimizer updates per scene.

Table 5 lists the shared configuration. Backbone forward passes use bfloat16, and trainable LoRA parameters are stored in float32. Reward networks are frozen and evaluated without gradient propagation through them.

A.2 Trajectory Sampling and Reward Measurement

Let zkz_{k} denote the generated latent variables at denoising step kk, cc the conditioning information, and σk\sigma_{k} the noise schedule. The stochastic Euler transition is

μθ​(zk,c)\displaystyle\mu_{\theta}(z_{k},c) =zk+(σk−1−σk)​vθ​(zk,c,σk),\displaystyle=z_{k}+(\sigma_{k-1}-\sigma_{k})v_{\theta}(z_{k},c,\sigma_{k}), (19)
ηk\displaystyle\eta_{k} =β​|σk−1−σk|​max⁡(σk,10−4)+10−4,\displaystyle=\beta\sqrt{|\sigma_{k-1}-\sigma_{k}|}\max(\sigma_{k},10^{-4})+10^{-4}, (20)
zk−1\displaystyle z_{k-1} =μθ​(zk,c)+ηk​ϵk,ϵk∼𝒩⁡(0,I).\displaystyle=\mu_{\theta}(z_{k},c)+\eta_{k}\epsilon_{k},\qquad\epsilon_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (21)

Trajectories within a group share their initial latent noise and use independent transition noise. We record the sampled transitions and their behavior-policy log densities for subsequent optimization.

For reward measurement, we decode the conditional mean of the final transition. This excludes the final noise injection from the scored video while retaining the effects of earlier stochastic transitions. Policy optimization uses the recorded stochastic transitions.

A.3 Advantage Computation and Policy Updates

Each reward component is normalized within the rollout group before the component advantages are combined. For component mm, let

μm=1G​∑i=1GRi,m,σm=1G​∑i=1G(Ri,m−μm)2.\mu_{m}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}R_{i,m},\qquad\sigma_{m}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}(R_{i,m}-\mu_{m})^{2}}. (22)

Using the fixed component weights αm\alpha_{m}, we compute

Ai=∑mαm 1[σm≥10−3]Ri,m−μmσm+10−6.A_{i}=\sum_{m}\alpha_{m}\,\mathbf{1}[\sigma_{m}\geq 10^{-3}]\frac{R_{i,m}-\mu_{m}}{\sigma_{m}+10^{-6}}. (23)

Components with standard deviation below 10−310^{-3} contribute zero to that group’s advantage. The same AiA_{i} is assigned to all denoising steps of trajectory ii.

For a generation region containing dd scalar latent variables, we use the mean Gaussian log density

ℓθ(zk−1∣zk,c)=−12​d∑j=1d[(zk−1,j−μθ,j)2ηk2+log(2πηk2)].\ell_{\theta}(z_{k-1}\mid z_{k},c)=-\frac{1}{2d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\left[\frac{(z_{k-1,j}-\mu_{\theta,j})^{2}}{\eta_{k}^{2}}+\log(2\pi\eta_{k}^{2})\right]. (24)

The ratio used in the clipped surrogate is

ρ~i,k=exp⁡(ℓθ−ℓθold),\widetilde{\rho}_{i,k}=\exp\!\left(\ell_{\theta}-\ell_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\right), (25)

with both densities evaluated at the same recorded transition. This is the 1/d1/d power of the corresponding joint density ratio. Behavior-policy log densities remain fixed during all four optimization passes on a group.

The resulting loss is

ℒPWM=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PWM}}={} −1G​K∑i=1G∑k=1Kmin(ρ~i,kAi,clip(ρ~i,k,1−εclip,1+εclip)Ai)\displaystyle-\frac{1}{GK}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\min\!\left(\widetilde{\rho}_{i,k}A_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\widetilde{\rho}_{i,k},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})A_{i}\right)
+λG​K∑i=1G∑k=1K‖μθ​(si,k)−μθ0​(si,k)‖22d.\displaystyle+\frac{\lambda}{GK}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\|\mu_{\theta}(s_{i,k})-\mu_{\theta_{0}}(s_{i,k})\|_{2}^{2}}{d}. (26)

The anchor compares transition means at the same denoising state. The frozen-base mean is obtained with the adapter disabled.

A.4 Adapter Checkpoint Averaging

We uniformly average the corresponding LoRA parameter tensors from the eight epoch checkpoints of each scene’s adaptation run. For a linear layer with pretrained weight W0W_{0}, write its adapted weight as W0+(α/r)​B​AW_{0}+(\alpha/r)BA. The delivered layer uses

A¯=18​∑e=18A(e),B¯=18​∑e=18B(e),WPWM=W0+αr​B¯​A¯.\overline{A}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{e=1}^{8}A^{(e)},\qquad\overline{B}=\frac{1}{8}\sum_{e=1}^{8}B^{(e)},\qquad W_{\mathrm{PWM}}=W_{0}+\frac{\alpha}{r}\overline{B}\,\overline{A}. (27)

Thus, averaging operates on the trainable adapter tensors; the resulting update is the product of their averages. The final model retains one rank-88 adapter. All eight checkpoints receive equal weight, and checkpoint construction uses no held-out test frames.

Appendix B Reward Definitions

Let x1:Lx_{1:L} be the reference support window and y1:Ly_{1:L} the generated video used for reward measurement, with L=29L=29. We specify the four components of the shared reward below. All reference quantities are computed from the current support window.

B.1 Feature Extraction and Temporal Aggregation

We use DINOv2-small for visual features, AlexNet-based LPIPS for perceptual distance, and RAFT-small (Teed and Deng, 2020) for optical flow. Images are resized to 224×224224\times 224 using bilinear interpolation with align_corners=False. DINOv2 inputs use ImageNet normalization with channel means (0.485,0.456,0.406)(0.485,0.456,0.406) and standard deviations (0.229,0.224,0.225)(0.229,0.224,0.225). LPIPS and RAFT inputs are mapped to [−1,1][-1,1].

Frame-wise appearance scores are aggregated as

𝒜(a1:L)=0.7L∑t=1Lat+0.3min1≤t≤Lat.\mathcal{A}(a_{1:L})=\frac{0.7}{L}\sum_{t=1}^{L}a_{t}+0.3\min_{1\leq t\leq L}a_{t}. (28)

The minimum term gives additional weight to the lowest-scoring frame within the window.

B.2 Reward Components

Scene feature fidelity.

Let fcls​(u)f_{\mathrm{cls}}(u) and fp​(u)f_{p}(u) denote the DINOv2 CLS feature and the feature at patch position pp, respectively. With PP patches, we compute

qt=\displaystyle q_{t}={} 0.3cos(fcls(yt),fcls(xt))\displaystyle 0.3\cos\!\left(f_{\mathrm{cls}}(y_{t}),f_{\mathrm{cls}}(x_{t})\right)
+0.7P∑p=1Pcos(fp(yt),fp(xt)),\displaystyle+\frac{0.7}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\cos\!\left(f_{p}(y_{t}),f_{p}(x_{t})\right), (29)
Rgt=\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{gt}}={} 𝒜(q1:L).\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(q_{1:L}). (30)

Patch features are paired at the same grid positions, combining global visual agreement with spatially localized feature agreement.

Perceptual appearance.

The perceptual component is

atlpips=1−LPIPS(yt,xt),Rlpips=𝒜(a1:Llpips).a_{t}^{\mathrm{lpips}}=1-\operatorname{LPIPS}(y_{t},x_{t}),\qquad R_{\mathrm{lpips}}=\mathcal{A}(a_{1:L}^{\mathrm{lpips}}). (31)

It assigns higher reward to frames with smaller perceptual distance from the reference.

Initial-frame consistency.

For the independent support windows used in adaptation, the reference visual state is the window’s ground-truth first frame:

Rcross=cos⁡(fcls​(y1),fcls​(x1)).R_{\mathrm{cross}}=\cos\!\left(f_{\mathrm{cls}}(y_{1}),f_{\mathrm{cls}}(x_{1})\right). (32)

This component anchors the generated window to its initial condition.

Motion magnitude matching.

Let F​(ut,ut+1)pF(u_{t},u_{t+1})_{p} be RAFT’s final flow prediction at pixel pp, and let Ω\Omega denote the resized pixel grid. Define

M(u1:L)\displaystyle M(u_{1:L}) =1(L−1)​|Ω|​∑t=1L−1∑p∈Ω‖F​(ut,ut+1)p‖2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(L-1)|\Omega|}\sum_{t=1}^{L-1}\sum_{p\in\Omega}\|F(u_{t},u_{t+1})_{p}\|_{2}, (33)
Rdyn\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{dyn}} =clip(1−|M(y1:L)−M(x1:L)|M(x1:L)+10−3,−1,1).\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(1-\frac{|M(y_{1:L})-M(x_{1:L})|}{M(x_{1:L})+10^{-3}},-1,1\right). (34)

This term rewards agreement in the average motion magnitude, penalizing both larger and smaller magnitudes relative to the support video. The four components enter the advantage calculation in Appendix A.3 with weights (0.50,0.30,0.10,0.10)(0.50,0.30,0.10,0.10).

Appendix C Evaluation Details

Our evaluation measures the benefit of adapting a pretrained world model to an individual scene. We compare each adapted model with native Yume on the same held-out continuation, then summarize both the magnitude and the distribution of scene-level benefits. This appendix specifies the paired evaluation, aggregation rules, and scoring implementation.

C.1 Paired Scene Continuations

Each scene provides a support trajectory for adaptation and a later, non-overlapping test trajectory for evaluation. PWM and Native use the same initial visual context, control sequence, native generation geometry, decoding configuration, and 145145-frame evaluation horizon. Native is evaluated with the scene adapter disabled. In the SFT comparison, the SFT adapter is evaluated under the same conditions.

We use the paired random seeds 𝒬={42,123,777}\mathcal{Q}=\{42,123,777\} with deterministic inference for each seed. Predictions are scored against the corresponding ground-truth test frames over the full horizon. The scene is the unit of aggregation: seed-level scores are averaged within a scene before results are combined across scenes.

C.2 Measuring Customization Benefit

Using Native as a common reference measures the value added by each adaptation method to the pretrained model. Let Ss,q(m)S_{s,q}^{(m)} denote the customization-fidelity score of method mm on scene ss with seed qq, where lower scores indicate closer agreement with the reference. The scene-level score is

S¯s(m)=1|𝒬|​∑q∈𝒬Ss,q(m).\overline{S}_{s}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}S_{s,q}^{(m)}. (35)

For m∈{PWM,SFT}m\in\{\mathrm{PWM},\mathrm{SFT}\}, define the absolute benefit and relative benefit as

Bs(m)\displaystyle B_{s}^{(m)} =S¯s(Native)−S¯s(m),\displaystyle=\overline{S}_{s}^{(\mathrm{Native})}-\overline{S}_{s}^{(m)}, (36)
Gs(m)\displaystyle G_{s}^{(m)} =100​S¯s(Native)−S¯s(m)S¯s(Native).\displaystyle=100\,\frac{\overline{S}_{s}^{(\mathrm{Native})}-\overline{S}_{s}^{(m)}}{\overline{S}_{s}^{(\mathrm{Native})}}. (37)

The relative benefit is defined for positive Native scores and is expressed as a percentage. Positive values indicate improvement; negative values indicate degradation. We first average the scores over seeds and then compute the relative benefit using that scene’s Native score. This expresses adaptation gains relative to the pretrained model’s error on each target scene.

C.3 Aggregation Across Scenes

For a domain containing the scene set 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we assign equal weight to every scene:

G¯𝒟(m)=1|𝒟|​∑s∈𝒟Gs(m).\overline{G}_{\mathcal{D}}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{D}}G_{s}^{(m)}. (38)

Overall aggregation applies the same rule to the union of the domain scene sets. PWM and SFT are summarized over the same paired scene set.

To define conditional summaries of degradation, consider the negative portion of each method’s scene-level benefit distribution. Let

𝒩m={s∈𝒟:Gs(m)<0}.\mathcal{N}_{m}=\{s\in\mathcal{D}:G_{s}^{(m)}<0\}. (39)

For nonempty 𝒩m\mathcal{N}_{m}, the conditional mean and median are

Gneg,mean(m)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{neg,mean}}^{(m)} =1|𝒩m|​∑s∈𝒩mGs(m),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}_{m}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{N}_{m}}G_{s}^{(m)}, (40)
Gneg,median(m)\displaystyle G_{\mathrm{neg,median}}^{(m)} =medians∈𝒩m⁡Gs(m).\displaystyle=\operatorname{median}_{s\in\mathcal{N}_{m}}G_{s}^{(m)}. (41)

These values retain their negative sign; values closer to zero indicate shallower degradation. The subset size |𝒩m||\mathcal{N}_{m}| counts scenes with negative benefit and is determined separately for each method. If no scene has negative benefit, these conditional statistics are undefined. The mean benefit and these conditional summaries jointly describe the scale of gains and regressions across scene customization tasks.

C.4 Scoring Implementation

Time-aligned appearance agreement.

We extract CLS features with facebook/dinov2-base, using its associated image processor. Let ϕ⁡(u)\phi(u) denote the ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized feature of frame uu. For generated frames g1:Tg_{1:T} and ground-truth test frames x1:Tx_{1:T}, with T=145T=145, we compute

Dpair=1T​∑t=1T(1−ϕ​(gt)⊤​ϕ​(xt)).D_{\mathrm{pair}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(1-\phi(g_{t})^{\top}\phi(x_{t})\right). (42)

Each frame is compared with the reference at the same timestep and contributes equally. This evaluates scene appearance as the controlled continuation unfolds. The evaluation uses DINOv2-base CLS features; the training reward in Appendix B uses DINOv2-small CLS and patch features.

Entity-class consistency.

The entity component measures the introduction of selected entity classes relative to the initial test frame. We use openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 with its associated processor and the fixed prompt pairs in Table 6. Let v⁡(u)v(u) be the normalized image embedding and ec+,ec−e_{c}^{+},e_{c}^{-} the normalized positive and negative text embeddings for class cc. The two-prompt CLIP score is

pc​(u)=exp⁡(100​v​(u)⊤​ec+)exp⁡(100​v​(u)⊤​ec+)+exp⁡(100​v​(u)⊤​ec−).p_{c}(u)=\frac{\exp\!\left(100\,v(u)^{\top}e_{c}^{+}\right)}{\exp\!\left(100\,v(u)^{\top}e_{c}^{+}\right)+\exp\!\left(100\,v(u)^{\top}e_{c}^{-}\right)}. (43)

For 𝒞={person,vehicle,animal}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathrm{person},\mathrm{vehicle},\mathrm{animal}\}, the initial frame determines the known-class indicators

bc=𝟏[pc(x1)>0.30].b_{c}=\mathbf{1}[p_{c}(x_{1})>0.30]. (44)

A generated frame is flagged if any class absent under this rule exceeds the generation threshold:

ht=[∃c∈𝒞:bc=0∧pc(gt)>0.50].h_{t}=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\exists c\in\mathcal{C}:b_{c}=0\ \land\ p_{c}(g_{t})>0.50\right]. (45)

The entity term and final score are

Dhall=1T​∑t=1Tht,S=Dpair+0.5​Dhall.D_{\mathrm{hall}}=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}h_{t},\qquad S=D_{\mathrm{pair}}+0.5D_{\mathrm{hall}}. (46)

Each frame contributes at most one entity flag, even if multiple classes trigger it. The same feature extractors, prompts, thresholds, and score weights are used for all compared methods.
